entry: American novelist, essayist, and countercultural figure. He considered himself a link between the Beat Generation of the 1950s and the hippies of the 1960s. His novel *One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest* (1962) was an immediate commercial and critical success. Some of Kesey's gatherings, known as Acid Tests, combined [[LSD]] with multimedia performances, and he mentored the [[Grateful Dead]]. He was imprisoned for five months in 1965 after being arrested for marijuana possession and faking suicide. He regarded *Sometimes a Great Notion* (1964), a novel about an Oregon logging family, as his magnum opus.

Nigerian writer, television producer, and social rights activist. Born in Bori near [[Port Harcourt]], he was a member of the Ogoni people, whose homeland, Ogoniland, in the Niger Delta had been targeted for crude oil extraction since the 1950s. As spokesperson, then president, of the Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People (MOSOP), he led a nonviolent campaign against environmental damage by oil companies, especially Royal Dutch Shell. A special military tribunal, which critics called irregular, tried him for allegedly masterminding the murder of Ogoni chiefs at a pro-government meeting. He was hanged by the military government of General Sani Abacha. His execution triggered international outrage and led to Nigeria's suspension from the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] for more than three years.

American rapper and songwriter. Rooted in West Coast [[Hip-hop]], his music features introspective lyrics and political and social commentary. Born and raised in Compton, [[California]], he signed with Top Dawg Entertainment in 2005. *Good Kid, M.A.A.D City* (2012), *To Pimp a Butterfly* (2015), and *Damn* (2017) were ranked among the greatest albums of all time by [[Rolling Stone]]. In 2018 he became the first musician outside the classical and jazz genres to receive the Pulitzer Prize for Music. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] listed him among the 100 most influential people in the world in 2016.

NASA field center on Merritt Island, Florida. Originally the NASA Launch Operations Center, it was renamed to honor President [[John F. Kennedy]]. Since 1968 it has been NASA's primary launch center for American spaceflight, research, and technology, handling launches for the Apollo, [[Skylab]], [[Space Shuttle]], and Artemis programs. Its 525-foot (160 m) Vehicle Assembly Building stacks NASA's largest rockets. Since 2010 the center has worked to become a multi-user spaceport through partnerships with [[SpaceX]] and [[Boeing]].

British actor and filmmaker. Born in [[Belfast]] and raised primarily in Reading, Branagh was knighted in 2012. He has directed and starred in film adaptations of [[William Shakespeare]]'s plays, including *Henry V* (1989), *Much Ado About Nothing* (1993), and *Hamlet* (1996). His semi-autobiographical film *Belfast* (2021) won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Original Screenplay. He received a Primetime Emmy Award for playing SS leader [[Reinhard Heydrich]] in the [[HBO]] film *Conspiracy* (2001).

Zambian politician, first president of Zambia (1964–1991). Kaunda led the United National Independence Party (UNIP), which organized nonviolent campaigns against colonial rule and the Central African Federation. Zambia became independent on October 24, 1964, and as president he promoted Zambian Humanism and nationalized copper mines and major industries. A constitutional amendment made UNIP the only legal party. Critics argue that his government became authoritarian, detaining opponents without trial, and that its economic policies, along with falling copper prices and the [[1973 oil crisis]], led to economic decline and mounting debt. Kaunda lost the 1991 multi-party elections to Frederick Chiluba. He positioned Zambia as a frontline state against minority rule in southern Africa, hosting liberation movements while maintaining non-alignment during the [[Cold War]].

American country music singer-songwriter. Rogers charted more than 120 hit singles and sold more than 100 million records worldwide. He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2013. His signature song, "The Gambler" (1978), won a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] and was selected in 2018 for preservation in the National Recording Registry by the [[Library of Congress]]. He recorded duets with [[Dolly Parton]] and had a songwriting partnership with [[Lionel Richie]]. Rogers co-founded the restaurant chain Kenny Rogers Roasters with former [[KFC]] CEO John Y. Brown Jr.

Ceremonial county in southeastern England (pop., 2024: 1,931,684). Covering 3,544 sq km, Kent is bordered by [[Essex]] across the Thames Estuary to the north and by [[Greater London]] to the northwest. The chalk ridge of the North Downs forms the White Cliffs of Dover, where it meets the [[English Channel]]. Kent's position between London and the Strait of Dover made it a point of entry for many figures in British history. In the 6th century, Saint Augustine landed there to begin the conversion of England to [[Christianity]] and became the first archbishop of Canterbury. Canterbury Cathedral is a [[World Heritage Site]].

Landlocked state in the southeastern United States (pop., 2024: approximately 4.6 million). Admitted to the Union as the 15th state on June 1, 1792, it had previously been part of [[Virginia]]. Its northern border is defined by the [[Ohio River]], and its capital is Frankfort. Kentucky bluegrass, a grass introduced by European settlers, has long supported the state's [[Thoroughbred]] horse industry. [[Tobacco]] has long been a major crop, while the economy has diversified into automobile manufacturing, energy production, and medicine. Mammoth Cave National Park contains the world's longest known cave system.

Japanese writer and Nobel laureate in literature (1994). Ōe was a major figure in contemporary [[Japanese literature]]. His novels, short stories, and essays, strongly influenced by French and American writing, address [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]], nuclear power, and [[Existentialism|existentialism]]. Born in a village on [[Shikoku]], he studied French literature at the [[University of Tokyo]] and was influenced by [[Jean-Paul Sartre]]. His father died in the [[Pacific War]]. His short story "Shiiku" (1958) won the Akutagawa Prize, and *Hiroshima Notes* (1965) explored nuclear devastation. His son Hikari, born in 1963, had lifelong developmental disabilities that shaped the theme of parental responsibility in his work. He was honored for creating "an imagined world, where life and myth condense to form a disconcerting picture of the human predicament today."

Exoplanet orbiting the Sun-like star Kepler-22. Discovered by [[NASA]]'s Kepler space telescope, it was announced on December 5, 2011, as the first known transiting planet to orbit within the habitable zone of a Sun-like star. It lies about 640 light-years from Earth in the constellation [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]]. Its radius is about twice that of Earth, but its mass and surface composition are unknown, and an Earth-like composition is considered unlikely. Scientists have dubbed it a "water world," though it may also have a volatile-rich composition. Its equilibrium temperature, assuming an Earth-like albedo, would be about 279 K (6 °C; 43 °F).

Disputed super-Earth exoplanet candidate orbiting the Sun-like star Kepler-452. Initial reports claimed it orbits within the inner edge of the habitable zone, and it is the only planet in its system discovered by the Kepler space telescope. Two later reports refuted the claim, but further work reestablished it. It lies about 1,800 light-years from Earth in the constellation [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]]. Its radius is around 1.63 times that of Earth, and it orbits at 1.04 AU with a period of roughly 385 days. It receives slightly more energy from its star than Earth and could experience a runaway greenhouse effect.

Type Ia supernova in the constellation [[Ophiuchus]]. Known as SN 1604, it appeared in October 1604 and is the most recent supernova in the Milky Way observed by the naked eye. At its peak it reached an apparent magnitude of −2.5, brighter than any other star in the night sky, and it was visible in daylight for over three weeks. [[Johannes Kepler]] began observing it on October 17 and tracked it for an entire year, though he was not its first observer. [[Galileo Galilei]] used it to challenge Aristotelian cosmology, prompting a dispute with Lodovico delle Colombe.

Three laws describing planetary orbits around the Sun. Published by [[Johannes Kepler]] from 1609 to 1621, they replaced the circular orbits and epicycles of Copernicus's heliocentric model with elliptical orbits, based on the accurate observations of [[Tycho Brahe]]. The first law states that each planet's orbit is an [[Ellipse|ellipse]] with the Sun at one focus. The second law states that equal areas are swept in equal times, so a planet moves faster when closer to the Sun. The third law states that the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit. Kepler's study of the orbit of [[Mars]] led him to infer that other bodies in the [[Solar System]] also move in ellipses. [[Isaac Newton]] later used the third law in deriving universal gravitation.

State on the Malabar Coast of southwestern India (pop., 2011: 33 million), officially Keralam. Formed in 1956 by unifying Malayalam-speaking regions, it has [[Thiruvananthapuram]] as its capital. Kerala is a strip of coastal plains between the [[Western Ghats]] and the Laccadive Sea, bordered by Karnataka and [[Tamil Nadu]]. Kerala has been a prominent exporter of spices since 3000 BCE. Black pepper and [[Natural rubber|natural rubber]] contribute significantly to national output, and [[Coconut|coconut]], [[Tea|tea]], [[Coffee|coffee]], and cashew are important crops. Kerala has the highest Human Development Index, literacy rate, and life expectancy in India, and its economy relies heavily on remittances from Malayali expatriates.

City in western Iran (pop., 2016: 946,651), capital of Kermanshah Province. It lies 525 km from [[Tehran]] in the Zagros Mountains. Founded in AD 390 by Bahram IV, the city was named for his title Kirmanshah, meaning King of Kerman, and later became capital of the [[Sasanian Empire]]. The area has been occupied since the [[Lower Paleolithic]], and the only Neanderthal skeletal remains found in Iran come from caves in the province. The [[Arabs]] conquered it in AD 629, and the Mongols under Hulegu sacked it in 1257. Nearby Taq-e Bostan preserves Sasanian-era rock reliefs, and the Behistun Inscription, carved by Darius I, is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]]. Its economy rests on oil refining, textiles, and livestock.

Core component of a computer [[Operating system|operating system]]. The kernel always has complete control over everything in the system, prevents and mitigates conflicts between processes, and remains resident in memory. It is usually one of the first programs loaded at startup, after the bootloader. The kernel controls hardware through device drivers, and application programs run in a separate user space so that malfunctioning programs cannot crash the entire operating system. Monolithic kernels such as [[Linux]] run entirely in one address space, while microkernels run most services in user space for resilience and modularity.

Combustible hydrocarbon liquid derived from [[Petroleum|petroleum]], also called paraffin. Its name derives from the Greek *kērós*, meaning wax, and Nova Scotia geologist Abraham Gesner registered it as a trademark in 1854 before the name became generic. It is widely used to power [[Jet engine|jet engines]] as jet fuel, and in a highly refined form called RP-1 it fuels some rocket engines. Kerosene is also used for cooking and lighting, and in parts of Asia it fuels small outboard motors and motorcycles. The [[World Health Organization]] considers it a polluting fuel because its smoke contains high levels of harmful particulate matter. Some U.S. jurisdictions, such as [[Pennsylvania]], require retail containers for kerosene to be blue, to distinguish it from gasoline.

Dissociative general anesthetic and NMDA receptor antagonist. It is used for short procedures in [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]] and, at lower doses, for pain and treatment-resistant [[Depression (mood)|depression]]. At anesthetic doses it preserves breathing and airway reflexes and usually stimulates the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]] rather than depressing it. It was first synthesized in 1962 as a derivative of [[Phencyclidine]] and approved in the United States in 1970. It was used extensively for surgical anesthesia in the [[Vietnam War]] and is regularly used in [[Veterinary medicine|veterinary medicine]]. It is tightly controlled because of recreational use, and it is contraindicated in severe heart or liver disease and uncontrolled [[Psychosis|psychosis]].

Sweet and sour table condiment, also spelled catsup. The term usually means tomato ketchup, made from tomatoes, sugar, and [[Vinegar|vinegar]] with spices such as [[Onion|onions]], [[Allspice]], [[Cumin]], and [[Garlic]]. Early recipes used mushrooms, oysters, and walnuts, and from the 1600s British ketchup was mainly made from mushrooms. The word first appeared in 1682, and its origin is unclear, with theories linking it to Hokkien words for fish brine and to the Malay *kicap*, meaning soy sauce. Tomato ketchup is a common condiment for hot, fried, or greasy foods. Mass production by the H.J. Heinz Company in the late 19th century helped make tomato ketchup dominant, with over 60% of the U.S. market.

Organic compound containing a carbonyl group (C=O) bonded to two carbon atoms. The simplest ketone is [[Acetone|acetone]], (CH₃)₂CO. The polar carbonyl group makes the carbon electrophilic, so nucleophiles add across the C=O bond to form alcohols and other derivatives. Because ketones cannot hydrogen-bond to themselves, they are more volatile than [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohols]] and [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acids]] of comparable molecular weight, which helps explain their use as solvents and in perfumery. Many ketones are important in biology and industry, including sugars, [[Steroid|steroids]] such as [[Testosterone]], and the solvent acetone. During fasting, the liver produces ketone bodies such as acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate from [[Fatty acid|fatty acid]] oxidation, supplying up to two-thirds of the brain's energy needs during starvation.

American actor and director. His breakthrough came in the musical-drama *Footloose* (1984), and he later starred in *JFK* (1991), *A Few Good Men* (1992), and *Apollo 13* (1995). For his role in the [[HBO]] film *Taking Chance* (2009), he received a Golden Globe Award and a Screen Actors Guild Award. He was honored with a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2003. He is associated with the concept of interconnectedness through the trivia game "Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon," which links actors by their shared films with him.

American actor, filmmaker, and musician. He rose to prominence with *The Untouchables* (1987), *Bull Durham* (1988), and *Field of Dreams* (1989). His western epic *Dances with Wolves* (1990), which he directed and starred in, won two [[Academy Awards]] for Best Picture and Best Director. He later directed *Open Range* (2003) and *Horizon: An American Saga* (2024). He won a Primetime Emmy Award for playing Devil Anse Hatfield in *Hatfields & McCoys* (2012) and played rancher John Dutton in the series *Yellowstone*. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2003. He fronts the country rock band Kevin Costner & Modern West.

Belgian professional footballer and midfielder. He made 422 appearances for Manchester City, winning six [[Premier League]] titles and the [[UEFA Champions League]] under manager [[Pep Guardiola]]. In 2017–18 he had a significant role in City becoming the only Premier League team to reach 100 points in a single season. He has played for Belgium since his debut in 2010, and he helped the team finish third at the 2018 [[FIFA World Cup]]. He was nominated for the Ballon d'Or, ending third in 2022. In June 2025 he joined [[Serie A]] club Napoli on a free transfer.

American basketball player for the Houston Rockets. Nicknamed "the Slim Reaper," Durant is widely regarded as one of the greatest scorers of all time and ranks fifth among [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] career scoring leaders. He was selected second overall by the Seattle SuperSonics in the 2007 NBA draft. He was named NBA MVP for 2013–14 and won two NBA championships and Finals MVP awards with the Golden State Warriors in 2017 and 2018. Durant has won four Olympic gold medals with Team USA in 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024, making him the only male basketball player to win four.
